topics.title: Prove these triangle theorems! (game)
topics.text:
Triangles have so many interesting properties. So I really wanted to make a game where we prove these triangle theorems. When lines in a triangle intersect, they seem to intersect at one point. And sometimes, there are interesting things happening with the picture! You can make your own proofs.



Theorem 1A: The perpendicular bisectors of the sides of every triangle are concurrent.



Proof 1A: Click to reveal hidden textThe perpendicular bisector of AB is the set of all points the same distance from A and B. At the same time, the perpendicular bisector of AC is the set of all points the same distance from A and C. Their intersection is in both sets, so the intersection is the same distance from A and B, and also the same distance from A and C. This point is the same distance from B and C, so it is on the perpendicular bisector of BC. Therefore, all three perpendicular bisectors of any triangle are concurrent.



Wait a minute! What if two of the perpendicular bisectors are parallel or coincide? Two of the perpendicular bisectors wouldn't intersect at one point, which means our proof wouldn't work!



To get around this, let the perpendicular bisector of AB be D, and let the perpendicular bisector of AC be E. D and E are both parallel. AB is perpendicular to D, AC is perpendicular to E, so A, B, and C are on a line with D and E perpendicular to them.



If D and E are the same, B and C are the same point. This means the the perpendicular bisector of BC is undefined.




Theorem 1B: The intersection of the perpendicular bisectors of a triangle is the circumcenter of the triangle.

Note: The circumcircle of a triangle is the circle that goes through all three vertices of the triangle. The circumradius is the radius of the circumcircle. The circumcenter is the center of the circumcircle.



Proof 1B: Click to reveal hidden textAs the intersection of the perpendicular bisectors are the same distance from A, B, and C, it is the circumcenter of the triangle. The circumcenter of degenerate triangles are undefined because it's so hard to get a circle through the vertices of the triangle.




Theorem 2A: The angle bisectors of the angles of a triangle are concurrent and intersect at exactly one point.



Proof 2A: Click to reveal hidden textThe angle bisector of angle A is the set of all points the same distance from AB and AC. To explain this better, let P be the angle bisector of BAC. If you take a point on P, label it X, X is the same distance from AB as it is from AC. No matter what X is, even if it's outside the triangle, it will be the same distance from AB and AC. The intersection of the angle bisectors of A and B must be the same distance from AB and AC, as well as the same distance from AB and BC. It is the same distance from AC and BC, so it is on the angle bisector of C.



Wait a minute! What if two of the angle bisectors are parallel or coincide? Two of the angle bisectors wouldn't intersect at one point, which means our proof wouldn't work!



I will label the angle bisectors of A, B, and C, P, Q, and R, respectively. Suppose P and Q were both parallel. Try to imagine where A, B, and C could go. I cannot seem to be able to place A, B, and C such that P and Q are parallel. Unfortunately, I do not have any better method of explaining this.



What about if P and Q coincide each other? Back with sliding A, B, and C around, I don't think this is possible. But it does seem possible with degenerate triangles. So the angle bisectors of any non-degenerate triangle are concurrent.




Theorem 2B: The intersection of the angle bisectors of a triangle is the incenter of the triangle.

Note: The incircle of a triangle is the circle that is tangent to all three sides and is inside the triangle. (it should be inside the triangle if it's tangent to all three sides) The inradius is the radius of the incircle. The incenter is the center of the incircle.



Proof 2B: Click to reveal hidden textThe intersection of the angle bisectors is the same distance from all three sides. So assuming that the intersection is the incenter, we draw the incircle. The incenter is the same perpendicular distance from the sides because tangent lines are perpendicular to the radius touching it. The definition of incenter matches the definition of the intersection of angle bisectors, so they are the same. The incircle of a degenerate triangle is practically a point, and a circle of radius 0.




The next 5 theorems assume X is the midpoint of AB, Y is the midpoint of AC, and Z is the midpoint of BC.



Theorem 3A: Prove that the medians of a triangle are concurrent and intersect at one point. The medians of triangle ABC are AZ, BY, and CX. Medians of triangles are lines going from a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side.



Proof 3A: Click to reveal hidden textNot knowing what I could do, I drew triangle XYZ inside triangle ABC. I noticed some very interesting facts, which are theorems 3B-3E. The next few proofs prove those. Amazingly, the medians of triangle ABC are also the medians of triangle XYZ! So the triangle inside XYZ using the midpoints of XYZ as its vertices has the same medians as XYZ and ABC. If I did this forever, I would get an infinitely small triangle with the same medians as ABC. Since any two medians intersect inside the triangle, any two of the three medians of this infinitely small triangle all intersect inside. The infinitely small triangle is basically a point, and the medians of the big triangle intersect inside the "point", so the medians are concurrent.




Theorem 3B: The line XY is parallel to BC.



Proof 3B: Click to reveal hidden textTriangles AXY and ABC are similar. This means angle AXY is the same as angle ABC. This means that XY is parallel to BC. Notice that angles AYX and ACB are also the same, we can prove XY is parallel to BC that way as well.




Theorem 3C: The line segment XY is half of BC.



Proof 3C: Click to reveal hidden textBy AXY being similar to ABC, and AXY being half of ABC, XY is half of BC.




Theorem 3D: Line AZ bisects XY.



Proof 3D: Click to reveal hidden textLet the intersection of AZ and XY be W. We see that AXW is similar to ABZ in a ratio 1:2. This tells us XW is half of BZ. And since BZ is half of BC, and XY is half of BC, XY is the same length as BZ. XW is half of BZ, so XW is half of XY and AZ bisects XY.




Theorem 3E: Two intersecting medians split each other in the ratio 2:1, with longer segment attached to the vertex.



Proof 3E: Click to reveal hidden textLet medians BY and CX intersect at I. Since BC is twice XY, and parallel, IXY is similar to ICB, with ICB being twice as big. IC is twice IX, and IB is twice IY, which is exactly what we want.




Theorem 4 is the altitudes are concurrent, but I couldn't prove this. Also, the theorems and proofs 3A-3E bounced into my head out of nowhere, no idea why.

topics.title: What is the answer?
topics.text:
So, I was doing my math quiz today, and there was a bonus question at the bottom. I did what I did, crunched numbers, calculated, and I got my answer. However, after I turned in my quiz, I talked with my other friends and we all had different answers. I was wondering if you guys could agree on one answer.



The problem is this: There are three cylinders stalked on one another. [This is not part of the problem, but since there is no image provided, I will add something.] Cylinder $A$ is on the top, Cylinder $B$ is in the middle, and Cylinder $C$ is at the bottom. All the cylinders have a height of 2 feet. Cylinder $A$ has a radius of 2 feet. Cylinder $B$ has a radius of 3 feet. Cylinder $C$ has a radius of 4 feet. Your job is to find the total surface area of the stacked cylinders. Do not include the bottom of Cylinder C as part of the surface area.



Let $\pi = 3.14$



IMAGE



A couple of handy hints to use:



Surface Area Formula for Cylinder$SA = 2\pi r h + 2\pi r^2$


A hint when solvingBe sure to subtract the parts of the cylinder that is overlapping with the other cylinders. Those parts are not considered to be part of the total surface area.






For this, I'm not asking for help on this problem, because I think I already know the answer. I just wanted to see how you guys would solve it and what you got. My friends and I just had differentiating answers, so I wanted to see which one was the right one.

topics.title: 2006 Cyprus MO/Lyceum/Problem 22
topics.text:
$AB\Gamma \Delta$ is rectangular and the points $K,\Lambda ,M,N$ lie on the sides $AB, B\Gamma , \Gamma \Delta, \Delta A$ respectively so that $\frac{AK}{KB}=\frac{BL}{L\Gamma}=\frac{\Gamma M}{M\Delta}=\frac{\Delta N}{NA}=2$. If $E_1$ is the area of $K\Lambda MN$ and $E_2$ is the area of the rectangle $AB\Gamma \Delta$, the ratio $\frac{E_1}{E_2}$ equals



$\mathrm{(A)}\ \frac{5}{9}\qquad\mathrm{(B)}\ \frac{1}{3}\qquad\mathrm{(C)}\ \frac{9}{5}\qquad\mathrm{(D)}\ \frac{3}{5}\qquad\mathrm{(E)}\ \text{None of these}$



Does anybody know the answer to this?



The solution on the website is Click to reveal hidden textLet $AB = \Gamma \Delta = x$, $B\Gamma = A\Delta = y$. Using the Pythagorean Theorem, $KM = \sqrt{\frac{x^2}{9} + y^2}$, $\Lambda N = \sqrt{x^2 + \frac{y^2}{9}}$. Using the formula $A = \frac{1}{2}d_1d_2$ for a rhombus, we get $\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{\left(x^2 + \frac{y^2}{9}\right)\left(x^2 + \frac{y^2}{9}\right)} = \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{\frac{x^4}{9} + \frac{y^4}{9} + \frac{82}{81}x^2y^2} = \frac{\sqrt{9x^4 + 9y^4 + 82x^2y^2}}{18}$. Thus the ratio is $\frac{\sqrt{9x^4 + 9y^4 + 82x^2y^2}}{18xy}$. There is no way we can simplify this further, and in fact we can plug in different values of $x,y$ to see that the answer is $\mathrm{E}$.



Be careful not to just try a couple of simple examples like $AB\Gamma \Delta$ being a square, where we will get the answer $5/9$, which is incorrect in general.




However, I don't know where the solution gets that the shape inside the rectangle is a rhombus and the solution itself.

I got 5/9 (A) without assuming that the shape inside the rectangle is a square.IMAGE

topics.title: Fixing Silly Mistakes
topics.text:
Okay, okay: This has obviously been discussed before, but I've read all the threads and the "Stop Making Stupid Mistakes" article. I think all those strategies will be very useful on the AMCs, but I was wondering about specifically MATHCOUNTS, where especially you need to go fast.



Last year I got a 33 on the State Competition, made the Connecticut team and then got a 24 at nationals. That was 143rd in the country. As a 7th-grader, I was pretty pleased with that result. But this year I want to do much better. Since nationals, I've been studying really hard, and I've consistently gotten 40s and above on practice State competitions. However, recently, now that I'm so close to a perfect score, what it takes to improve means nothing about how much math I know: it's about avoidance of those stupid silly mistakes. No matter what I try, they stay there. Work my Sprint score up to a consistent 28 or above? Great, next day I get a 6/8 on the Target. They just won't go away. I've tried countless strategies to avoid silly mistakes, including doing every question twice, underlining words, and even reading the questions out loud (silently, of course). All these strategies help me, but then they stop working and are no use except for slowing me down. Recently, on practice tests, old or new, I've gotten many scores in the 35-40 range, lower than I previously got on practice tests. So not only have these strategies not worked, they've actually made me worse. I've been doing practice on MATHCOUNTS Trainer, and the way I practice is by doing 5 problems at a time, using a calculator only for questions that say "decimal to the nearest tenth" etc. I haven't gotten 5/5 at any level in a very long time. The silly mistakes are coming back too strong.



I know from experience that I usually respond to threads like this with advice, but this time it's my turn to ask advice from the wonderful group of experienced contest-takers at AoPS. What should I do to minimize silly mistakes and what has worked for you in the past in this situation?



Thanks so much,



rafa2be

topics.title: Some math problems
topics.text:
1. Alex and Gene are painting a fence. Alex can paint a fence alone in eight hours. Gene can paint a fence alone in $12$ hours. If Gene starts painting the fence at $1:00$ p.m. and Alex joins at $3:00$ p.m., what time will they finish painting the fence?



My solutionGene will be painting the fence alone for $2$ hours, so he finished $\frac{2}{12}=\frac{1}{6}$ of the fence, so their is $\frac{5}{6}$ of the fence left. When Alex came, Alex can paint $\frac{1}{8}$ of the fence in an hour and Gene can finish $\frac{1}{12}$ of the fence in an hour. Since they are working together, they work at $\frac{1}{12}+\frac{1}{8}=\frac{5}{24}$ together. Since we are finding how much time it will take, we will make a variable $t$ standing for time. So we now have an equation $\frac{5t}{24}=\frac{5}{6}$. Solving for $t$, we get $t=4$, so it will take $4$ hours for them finish. Adding $4$ to $3:00$p.m., they will finish painting the fence at $7:00$p.m.




2. A car takes $30$ minutes to go to a hospital on a $15$ mile road, and a supersonic jet takes $2$ minutes to fly to the same hospital on a $10$ mile airway. However, it takes $10$ minutes to fill its engine, and $5$ minutes to find a landing spot. Who will finish first and by how much minutes?



My solutionIf it takes $10$ minutes to fill the engine and $5$ minutes to find a landing spot, it takes a total of $15$ minutes to do them both. We want to see how much minutes it takes for it by itself without either to go to the hospital. So we subtract $15$ from $30$ giving the car only $15$ minutes to go to the hospital, and $2$ minutes for the jet to fly to the hospital. So the supersonic jet beats the car by $13$ minutes.

topics.title: 2016 AMC 10A Problem 17
topics.text:
Source: AoPS Wiki

ProblemLet $N$ be a positive multiple of $5$. One red ball and $N$ green balls are arranged in a line in random order. Let $P(N)$ be the probability that at least $\tfrac{3}{5}$ of the green balls are on the same side of the red ball. Observe that $P(5)=1$ and that $P(N)$ approaches $\tfrac{4}{5}$ as $N$ grows large. What is the sum of the digits of the least value of $N$ such that $P(N) < \tfrac{321}{400}$?



$\textbf{(A) } 12 \qquad \textbf{(B) } 14 \qquad \textbf{(C) }16 \qquad \textbf{(D) } 18 \qquad \textbf{(E) } 20$


SolutionLet $n = \frac{N}{5}$. Then, consider $5$ blocks of $n$ green balls in a line, along with the red ball. Shuffling the line is equivalent to choosing one of the $N + 1$ positions between the green balls to insert the red ball. Less than $\frac{3}{5}$ of the green balls will be on the same side of the red ball if the red ball is inserted in the middle block of $n$ balls, and there are $n - 1$ positions where this happens. Thus, $P(N) = 1 - \frac{n - 1}{N + 1} = \frac{0.8N + 2}{N + 1}$. Solving the inequality $P(N) = \frac{0.8N + 2}{N + 1} < \frac{321}{400}$ gives $N > 479$, so the least value of $N$ is $480$. The sum of the digits of $480$ is $\boxed{12}$.

topics.title: Distance Formula Argument
topics.text: When I was at school, I had an conversation with a geometry student. We were talking about the Distance Formula. I commented on how the Pythagoras Theorem and the Distance Formula relate to each other. He began to say that they didn't relate each other because their formulas are different, saying the Pythagoras theorem is a^2 + b^2 = c^2 and how distance formula is completely different to that formula. Then I said they can the distance formula can be interpreted and is like the Pythagoras theorem and then he still said no kept on saying that they're nothing alike. Then when I said the distance formula is the square root of (y2 - y1)^2 + (x2 - x1)^2 = distance, he said that's wrong and x should go first not y, it only works like that for slope. I start to wonder if this kid who apparently has an 98% in geometry, understands anything he's taught. I feel as if he is the type of guy that would remember the quadratic formula and not it's proof. So who's right on this?
